# Cat clogging with the wrong plugs

It is a classic case of "garbage in, garbage out," but applied to an internal combustion engine rather than a data pipeline. You replaced the ignition components on your 2010 Mazda 3 2.0L with NGK plugs advertised as "pre-gapped." While modern manufacturing aims for consistency, assuming the factory gap is perfect without measuring it is a risky heuristic. When you measured the gaps and found them consistent with the 2.3 turbo modelsâlikely around 0.7mm instead of the standard 1.1mm to 1.3mm range required for your naturally aspirated engineâyou identified a mismatch in ignition timing physics.

Under-gapping an engine restricts the spark arc length, forcing the ECU to advance timing or lean out the mixture to compensate, but often resulting in incomplete combustion events. This creates a rich exhaust stream relative to what the catalytic converter expects. The fact that you didn't get a misfire code (P030x) is typical; the ECU usually flags a misfire only when unburnt fuel exceeds a specific threshold during active ignition, whereas a slightly under-gapped plug might just run "hot" and lean-rich in a way that doesn't trigger the OBD-II logic immediately.

Your observation about the harsh cold idle suggests the engine is struggling to stabilize combustion at low loads. When you bent the plugs back into shape (mechanically widening the gap), you improved low-speed acceleration, which aligns with better spark energy transfer. However, the behavior when letting off the accelerator at highway speedsâRPMs spiking up like a slipping transmissionâis a distinct red flag for exhaust flow restriction.

Could this be a clogged catalytic converter? Yes, and there is a direct causal link to your plug installation. Running an engine with under-gapped plugs promotes incomplete combustion, pumping excess hydrocarbons (HC) into the exhaust system. The catalytic converter relies on a precise air-fuel ratio (typically around 14.7:1) to function efficiently. When you flood it with rich mixtures caused by poor ignition efficiency, the internal substrates can melt or become coated with unburnt fuel deposits much faster than expected. This effectively clogs the honeycomb structure, increasing backpressure.

The transient P0455 (gross leak) code is interesting in this context. Sometimes, a severely restricted exhaust system creates enough pressure differential to confuse the EVAP monitoring logic, or the vacuum leaks associated with engine hesitation are misread as an evaporative system fault. Since the code cleared and didn't return immediately, it suggests the issue was intermittent or related to the transient nature of the rich burn rather than a permanent physical breach in the lines.

To confirm this without disassembling the exhaust manifold, you need objective data on backpressure. A simple visual inspection is rarely enough for a clogged cat; the converter can be 50% blocked and still look normal from the outside. The most reliable low-tech test involves checking the oxygen sensor voltage history or, better yet, performing a vacuum test at idle. If the manifold vacuum drops significantly under load compared to a healthy engine, backpressure is likely high.

You can also use an OBD-II scanner to pull live data for Short Term Fuel Trim (STFT) and Long Term Fuel Trim (LTFT). On your Mazda, if you see positive fuel trims exceeding +10% or +20%, the ECU is actively adding more fuel to compensate for a lean condition elsewhere, but in this specific scenario of rich exhaust, you might actually see negative trims if the O2 sensor is being flooded with hydrocarbons. Waitâcorrection: if the cat is clogged and hot, the O2 sensor downstream (Sensor 2) will likely show little to no activity because it's starved of fresh oxygen due to the blockage. A flat line on Sensor 2 while Sensor 1 fluctuates normally is a definitive sign of a failed or plugged converter.

Once you verify the backpressure or confirm the O2 sensor lack of switching, replacing the catalytic converter will likely resolve the harsh idle and the RPM spike upon throttle release. The "slipping transmission" feel is just the engine fighting against the restriction in the exhaust path, causing torque loss and erratic load shedding. It is a reminder that even minor hardware substitutions, like spark plugs, can have cascading effects on downstream components if the installation parameters aren't strictly verified.
